Joseph Kosinski's dream is the dream of 'non-political art', and it is a dream that he shares with thousands, no, millions, worldwide. The subject has been up for debate in the past, many hundreds of years before its most recent formulation in the X/Twitter-hosted 'is this cute anime girl eating a sandwich political?'-debate, seemingly with no real answer. Top Gun: Maverick is probably his most daring and edgy attempt at 'non-political art', confronting the problem at its home turf, the US military-propaganda film, trying his darndest to squeeze out a pleasure-only feature film about the US Navy pilots simply being Good At Their Jobs. For this, he mined narrative resources from rich deposits such as the 'Call of Duty' and 'Battlefield' franchises, and using their lessons, managed to construct what has now become the 2020s blockbuster-darling, the 'rebirth' of Cinema as many have now come to call it. Vietnam, Korea, Afghanistan, Iraq, these are names of the old-world, no longer relevant in the realm of superstar Tom 'Maverick' Cruise; in his domain, using only the film's own terminology, there are now only nameless 'Enemies', 'Rogue States' protected by faceless 'Bandits', states which pose a threat to 'Allies' in a quite unspecific 'Region' of the world by refining Uranium and therefore breaking with 'Conventions' and 'Rules'... but worry not, this is all Gameplay, it is W Fiction, it is literally Cinema—there surely isn't an ongoing military campaign that matches 1:1 with the film—and any tinge of worry or instinctual disgust will be washed away by the booms of jet-engines, your lingering worries will be sedated by Tom Cruise's charismatic smile, and any fear you may have that things could EVER go wrong will be extinguished by having the pleasure of witnessing America's men (and women! Thank you, 21st century.) doing a damn good job!

A big dumb movie like Top Gun deserves a big dumb sequel,  otherwise the entire endeavor doesn't seem worthwhile. Maverick doesn't go far enough in that direction. I'm of the mind that most of this is fine, if uninspired. However, Kelly McGillis not returning, and rather slotting Jennifer Connely into a new character role, is a terrible choice that feels retrofitted around the absence of the romance from the first movie. Like many late career Tom Cruise romances on film, it feels perfunctory at best and carries no weight. Similarly, Miles Teller unfortunately lacks the charisma of his onscreen deceased father,  Anthony Edwards/Goose. Disappointed in the young recruits' call signs: Playback; Hangman; Rooster; boring.I wish they'd have gotten weirder with it: Doghat; Flip-Flop; Groundswell; etc There's nothing as interesting as Iceman, here. All of the new recruits mostly feel like hollow proxys of characters from the original, most glaringly Glen Powell. It's bad criticism to say what you'd prefer the movie to be about rather than what it is,  and I'm anti-deaging effects in onscreen generally, because they seldom look good, but the opening of this movie,  Tom Cruise flying mach 10+ in a fancy future jet,  made me think that a plot where he accidentally flies into the past, back to the 80s, and saves a de-aged Anthony Edwards from death, maybe even bringing him back to the 2020s, would rule. Overall lacking the blissed out stupidity of the original.  Disappointing it doesn't lean harder into some legacy aspects, namely musically. Kind of insane not to do a Danger Zone needledrop. Possibly just in need of a Tony Scott infusion that is sadly no longer possible. Jets are very cinematic.

A movie that only gets more disappointing the more you watch it. Maverick completely lacks the nuance and beauty of the original film. All the love has been drained out in favor of vague foreign threats and fancam fodder. Every time the story is presented with the opportunity to do something interesting, it decides instead to go in the most bland direction possible. In Maverick grief is smoothed over and easily forgotten. In the first film, our heroes were fallible - grief forced them into their own personal reckonings. Not even the US government can save men from their feelings, and that creates a compelling and relatable narrative. In Maverick, the heroes exist only to kill faceless bad guys and always make it out alive. Freedom fighters can never die. There is no questioning the protagonists and no sympathizing with the antagonists. When nothing bad can happen, the franchise cannot be anything more than a spineless advertisement with facist undertones, and I truly believe it has the capacity to be more than that. The more friends ask me to watch this movie with them, the more I find it hard to ignore its glaring faults. I’d just rather be watching the original. I love Tom Cruise and I love action movies; I know that they are capable of more.

“This made me so hard” (He said as a sarcastic jab at the over the top ineffective attempt to evoke a certain set of feelings) I think I did an ok job making fun of this movie in a paper I wrote to some youth I mentor, so I’ll just attach a bit of that. My recent reflection, the basis of writing such a dissentful-sounding paper as this, came along with an experience that I believe we’ve all had. I watched a bad piece of media and got a bit too upset over it. After reflection, though, I do believe that “Top Gun: Maverick” has value past its admittedly wonderful cinematography. We can use it as a reminder of why we are what we are in our organization. In speaking about this reminder, I hope that I can convince you to hold a mirror up to yourself, your priorities, and your intentions. Sunglasses. Fighter jets. Motorcycles. Motorcycles driving alongside fighter jets with drivers wearing sunglasses and no helmet. What do these things have in common? We are made to think that they’re very cool. Let’s ignore how ridiculous the opening to that paragraph is, and instead use it as an allegory. Even though Maverick is the “very cool” hero and is one of the world's best pilots, he is the blatant epitome of a bad leader and a bad follower. He directs his training exercises in ways that serve only to stroke his own ego. He ignores multiple direct commands from his superiors and even throws away major safety boundaries without purpose. He doesn’t even learn from his mistakes, instead choosing to continue to endanger those around him. Despite this, we are made to idolize him. The entire film is an embarrassing attempt to make a piece of media about a certain type of disciplined person, while containing character development that entirely destroys what is means to be that person.

One Star For Heart-Racing Action One more star for Jennifer Connelly This is a peculiar one, it’s clearly propaganda, but the writers seem keenly aware of this fact, and try to some effectiveness to make the enemy so opaque as to walk on eggshells to avoid being overtly hateful or targeted. So ultimately what you’ve got is military propaganda that is half baked. The cinematography carries most of the weight here.

Mini-collab with Dan (who also convinced me to watch the OG, kudos to Dan) Watched literally right after rewatching Top Gun , and I know I'm in the minority here, but I did not like this as much. The magic of Top Gun is gone. What made the OG special was its coming of age story. The focus was on Maverick. Of course the sequel's title is Maverick , but the thing is, Maverick got his arc in the first film. Instead of passing the torch on to the young generation, the film doesn't dare do so, instead rewinding and resetting Maverick's major arc beats. This is as per course of a series, but it still makes it no less lazy, especially when Cruise is pushing 60. Maverick's very much an outsider and he needs a new romance which adds even less to the sum than the original (while absolutely trashing McGillis's Charlie by not even giving her a passing mention from anyone , I'm not even going to pretend Maverick is in any way hung up on her after so many years, so they could've had anyone mention her). Sure, there's new blood, Rooster and Hangman (Glen Powell was a mix of Iceman and Maverick somehow for me), but the spotlight's still on Maverick. Glen Powell didn't have enough screentime, but then again, he wasn't the most important of the recruits, but even Miles Teller's Rooster felt side-lined. It's telling that the focus of training was Maverick. Can the recruits outmanoeuvre him, can he simulate bombing (Iran-- ahem-- I mean--) an unnamed nuclear enrichment site under the deadline? The visuals match the OG at the beginning, but gradually slip into ugly modern lensing. The music is nostalgia bait and not as strong. Even the greater focus on the mission with its target specifics lent a darker tone. At a point earlier on, Maverick makes a comment to Jon Hamm's character that he's going to train the kids to return only to be met with an incredulous stare. The connotation was clear. They're training pilots for suicide missions. Meeting the objective is the most important and only goal. The original film was an entirely different vibe. Maverick felt modern in the worst ways for me, including sacrificing character and connection for plot beats and seriousness. Basically, I don't think the sequel brought anything fresh or better; it was entirely of its 2020s generation. I suppose I got to watch Glen Powell in another film. Yay?

É um ótimo exercício de marketing, com cenas de caça que tiram o fôlego. E só! A sessão nostalgia tem agradado muito ao público nos últimos anos. Filmes que fizeram sucesso nos anos 80, 90 e até no início dos anos 2000 estão ganhando cada vez mais remakes, reboots ou, como neste caso, continuações. Há muitos críticos dizendo que Top Gun: Maverick é “maravilhoso”, uma “correção do passado”. No caso das cenas de voo, eu até concordo. São impressionantes e, sem dúvida, o grande destaque do filme. Mas todo o restante acaba sendo prejudicado pela repetição de trilha sonora — com exceção da música-tema, que continua linda —, de cenas e até de um contexto muito semelhante ao primeiro filme, tudo cuidadosamente pensado para manter os saudosistas encantados. Assim como no primeiro Top Gun , não temos um roteiro muito elaborado. Em alguns momentos, a história se mostra confusa, enquanto os personagens são explorados de maneira superficial. O próprio nome Maverick faz jus ao filme: tudo gira em torno dele. O maior destaque é, mais uma vez, Tom Cruise. Parece que o filme foi concebido também para mostrar que, mais de 30 anos depois, ele ainda consegue tirar o fôlego do público com suas performances — seja na moto, no caça ou simplesmente demonstrando um vigor e uma energia que continuam sendo sua marca registrada. Top Gun: Maverick entrega um espetáculo visual impressionante e cumpre muito bem a missão de despertar a nostalgia. Mas, quando retiramos todo esse aparato, sobra pouco além de uma continuação que se apoia demais no passado para funcionar no presente.

Eine weiterführung des Films aus den 1980ern. Wir begleiten wieder Maverick, der immer noch Captain der Navy ist bei seiner Arbeit. Er hat nun eine Stelle als Testpilot für die Navy und testet eine neues Flugzeug, das den Überschallflug revoluzionieren soll. doch das Militär will die teure Entwicklung eines solchen Flugzeugs nicht mehr unterstützen. Um zu beweisen, dass das Flugzeug es wert ist, dass daran weitergeforscht werden darf riskiert er den ersten Flug mit Mach 10. Als er aber noch mehr aus der Maschine herauskitzeln will passiert es. Das Flugzeug gerät ins Schlingern und stürzt ab. Da er nun seine Job verloren hat, wird er erneut dem Top Gun-Stützpunkt, diesmal als Trainer zugeteilt. Hier soll er die jungen Wilden auf einen tödlichen Einsatz vorbereiten. Unter den Piloten ist auch der Sohn von Goose, dem Co-Piloten, der damals bei einem Einsatz mit Maverick ums Leben kam. Der Film glänzt, wie schon damals mit unglaublich guten Bildern, die das amerikanische Militär nur von seiner besten Seite zeigt. Das versucht der Film aber auch nicht im Ansatz zu verheimlichen. Die Musik lässt einen sofort wieder izurückerinnern an das Original. Ein Film, der nur so von Testosteron strotzt, das Original hochhält und weiterführt.
